performers: Pierre Mollet, baritone; women of the Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: Boulanger’s Psalm 129, “Ils m’ont assez opprimé dès ma jeunesse”, is a psalm of persecution and defiance in which Pierre Mollet sings after an orchestral opening marked Grave, rude. The women’s voices enter only at the close, accompanied by celesta, harp and muted strings.

sections.label: Intro · Woodwind and horn chords, plucked basses
sections.mNote: Accented woodwind and horn chords begin the D minor psalm.

sections.label: A · First baritone entry
sections.mNote: The voice holds over descending figures in the strings.

sections.label: B · Triplets in the clarinets
sections.mNote: The clarinets play triplets above the slower bass and voices.

sections.label: Coda · Women’s voices and celesta
sections.mNote: The women enter softly above harp and muted strings.

cues.title: Orchestral introduction, Grave, rude
cues.text: Grave, rude: solemn and rough. Woodwinds and horns play accented long chords over pizzicato double basses, and the violins, violas and cellos rest. The orchestra plays for thirty bars before the voice enters.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10382 (1924), p. 1 and orchestral introduction through p. 7. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sarrusophone in the bass
cues.text: The score lists a sarrusophone after the bassoons. It is a double-reed instrument made in several sizes, and here it serves as a bass. Boulanger places it beneath the bassoons and the upper horn, and Helen Julia Minors has cited it as an example of her use of orchestral colour.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, instrument list (printed p. 3): https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Helen Julia Minors, preface to Psalm 129 (2011): https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html

cues.title: Entry of the baritone
cues.text: Pierre Mollet’s baritone enters with the psalm’s words on oppression endured since youth. While the voice holds its notes, descending figures pass from the violins down through the violas and cellos to the double basses.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 8, figure 3: opening vocal phrase and descending string figures. The score permits solo baritone in place of the printed male-chorus parts; Mollet is credited on this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ploughmen verse, figure 4
cues.text: The psalm text at this point says that ploughmen cut furrows into the speaker’s back. Clarinets and bass clarinet move up and down in triplets. Beneath them the bass rises slowly, and the voice sings its complaint in long notes.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 11, figure 4, setting Des laboureurs ont labouré mon dos; clarinet triplets and rising lower parts. Helen Julia Minors, preface (2011). https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1921
cues.text: In 1921 Henri Büsser conducted the first performance at the Salle Pleyel in Paris, for the Concerts Dandelot. Boulanger had died three years earlier. She had finished the score in Rome in 1916.
cues.evidence: Helen Julia Minors, preface to Psalm 129 (Musikproduktion Höflich, 2011), gives the 1916 composition and 1921 première. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html

cues.title: Georges Migot, La revue musicale, 1924
cues.text: Writing in La revue musicale in 1924, Georges Migot heard in the chord progressions “the dull hatred and exasperated anger of an oppressed people”. The psalm opens with the words “Ils m’ont assez opprimé dès ma jeunesse” (they have oppressed me since my youth).
cues.evidence: Migot’s French, “Les progressions mâles et puissantes expriment la haine sourde et la colère exaspérée d’un peuple opprimé”, as quoted in Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011); our translation. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html

cues.title: Coda, women’s voices
cues.text: The coda slows at figure 8, marked Un peu plus lent. Women’s voices enter ppp on “Ah”, high above the continuing prayer, with flute and celesta doubling their line. The strings are muted, and the harp plays beneath dissonant chords.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 22–24, figure 8: Un peu plus lent, women’s voices marked ppp on Ah, flute, celesta, harp and muted strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performance options in the score
cues.text: Boulanger’s score allows a baritone soloist with optional women’s voices, a men’s chorus, or a mixed chorus. Here Pierre Mollet sings the baritone part. A printed note asks the conductor to keep the brass below the written dynamics when a soloist sings.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed p. 3, performance options and note: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Everest LPBR 6059 sleeve names Pierre Mollet, baritone: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d

cues.title: Final bars, wordless voices
cues.text: The final vocal phrase has no words. Divided strings hold soft chords, and horn, bassoon and harp play short solo figures between them. The dissonances are not resolved as the last notes die away.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 25, final four bars: wordless voices, sustained divided strings and solo instrumental replies. Helen Julia Minors’s preface describes the unresolved closing dissonances.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Opening chords return beneath the voice
transitions.from: Intro · Woodwind and horn chords, plucked basses
transitions.how: The opening chords return beneath the first vocal phrase, marked a Tempo, grave et rude. The winds hold their accented harmony and the strings play quick figures. While the baritone holds the end of his phrase, a five-note run passes down through the string sections to the double basses.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 7–8, figure 3; Helen Julia Minors (2011) identifies the return of the introduction’s chord progression beneath the voice.

transitions.title: Clarinets begin their triplets
transitions.how: At figure 4 the clarinets and bass clarinet begin continuous triplets. Bassoons, horns, harp and low strings rise more slowly beneath them. The baritone also begins with a triplet, then sets the words in longer notes over the clarinets’ running triplets; the vocal part is marked contenu, restrained.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 11, figure 4: clarinet triplets, ascending bass and contenu vocal phrase.

transitions.title: Celesta and voices above the bass
transitions.how: Un peu plus lent slows the coda, and the metre alternates between four crotchets and three minims. The bass descends in long notes beneath a solo harp figure. Women’s voices, flute and celesta take the upper line. The horns and strings are muted.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 21–22, figure 8: tempo and metre changes, descending bass, solo harp, women’s voices and celesta; muting instructions for horns and strings.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Psaume CXXIX, Durand full score (1924), plate D. & F. 10382
source.locator: Prefatory performance options and printed pp. 1, 5, 8, 11, 16, 21–25. The score permits a solo baritone with women’s voices, as on this recording. At figure 6 the baritone version reduces the trumpet and trombone parts. The orchestra includes two harps and sarrusophone.

timeline.note: Accented winds and horns sound above plucked double basses. The other strings rest.
Violins and cellos hold long notes while violas and clarinets repeat their shorter figures.
Pierre Mollet’s baritone enters at figure 3. Descending string figures answer the vocal phrase.
Clarinets and bass clarinet play triplets beneath the voice at figure 4.
The opening phrase returns at figure 6, with the voice marked clamant. The baritone version uses one trumpet and one trombone for the first six bars.
Women’s voices enter very softly at figure 8, with celesta and harp. The strings put on mutes.
The women hold wordless chords above muted strings. Harps, celesta and quiet winds play the closing phrases.

composer.epithet: Composer who won the Prix de Rome at nineteen and, before her death at twenty-four, wrote songs of lost love and settings of psalms.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
In May 1913 five young composers were shut away at the Château de Compiègne, writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent them champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Lili Boulanger was one of the signatories. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome, because illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the thirty-six voters of the Académie des Beaux-Arts supported her. Faust et Hélène is scored for a tenor Faust in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, with a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
